1. Lead on this: 562 horsepower at 9,000 rpm from four and a half litres, with no turbochargers anywhere. Open on the revs and the power together - the 9,000 is the number. Do not name the make or the model in the first sentence, and do not open on the price.

2. The core argument, and it is the reason this car matters: when it launched, no naturally aspirated road car engine had ever made more power per litre - about 125 horsepower from every litre. Then the car that replaced it went twin-turbo. The 488 makes more power from a smaller 3.9-litre engine and stops revving sooner, and it was the first mid-engined turbo Ferrari since the F40. So this is the last naturally aspirated mid-engined V8 Ferrari there will ever be. Verify the specific-output claim and the F40 line independently.

3. Cover the catch, and get the nuance right rather than scaring people off. The famous one is the 2010 fire recall: the adhesive holding the rear wheel-arch liners could overheat and catch fire on a car driven hard in hot weather, and Ferrari recalled 1,248 cars built before July 2010 and replaced the glue with mechanical fasteners. This car is a 2011, so it is almost certainly outside that window - say that, do not imply this car is affected. The real checks on one of these are confirming the campaign work was done against the VIN and looking at the rear arches for corrosion, which runs four figures per arch to put right properly.

4. The reputation beat is the gearbox, so write it as the argument people have: seven-speed dual-clutch, and Ferrari never offered a manual on this car at all. Verify that before stating it. If it holds, that is the thing enthusiasts still argue about - the most highly strung naturally aspirated V8 Ferrari ever built, and you cannot have three pedals in it.

5. Cover the name and the cabin in one beat. The number is literal: 4.5 litres and 8 cylinders. The steering wheel carries every control - indicators, wipers, the starter, the manettino - because Ferrari copied its own Formula One practice and left the column bare. Credit the design studio rather than naming an individual designer, and verify which studio it was.

6. Close on the question: would you take 9,000 rpm and no turbos, or more power from the turbocharged one that replaced it?

sections.Highlights: THIS... is a 2011 Ferrari 458 Italia, finished in Rosso Corsa with a tan interior. This 458 Italia is equipped with a full Mansory Siracusa body kit. The odometer on this Ferrari currently indicates approximately 4,000 miles. The attached Carfax vehicle history report lists no accidents or mileage discrepancies in this Ferrari's past. It also confirms California registration from new. A partial list of notable equipment reported by the seller includes Brembo carbon ceramic brakes with red calipers, Scuderia Ferrari shields on the fenders, leather upholstery, power-adjustable seats, and a Manettino carbon fiber steering wheel. In addition to the Mansory body kit, notable modifications reported by the seller include 20-inch front and 21-inch rear Mansory wheels. Ferrari's new models come in two flavors: evolutionary and revolutionary. Released for 2010, the 458 Italia fell in the latter category with aluminum chassis parts and body panels, a minimalist interior that ditched even the turn signal stalks, and a new engine mounted behind the passengers. It was launched as Ferrari's fastest and highest-revving V8-powered production car, and it remained in production until 2015. The 458 and all of its variants would be the final naturally-aspirated V8 cars produced by the company before switching to turbocharged units with the introduction of the 488. Mansory is a luxury automotive customization company that specializes in bespoke vehicle modifications, including custom body kits, interior redesigns, performance upgrades, and extensive carbon-fiber craftsmanship. Founded in 1989 by Kourosh Mansory, the company is known for bold styling, distinctive visual details, and highly individualized finishes. Power comes from a 4.5-liter V8, rated at 562 horsepower and 398 lb-ft of torque. Part of the F136 family of engines, it spins the rear wheels via a 7-speed dual-clutch transmission.
